```{python setup}

import os

sys.path.append('.')

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from notes_style import (use_chapter, save, tidy, arrow_down,
                         INK, LOADCLR, REACTCLR, DIMCLR,
```

We now know

::: {.derivation}
$$
(\mathrm{S}) \Longleftrightarrow (\mathrm{W})
\;\overset{\text{approximate}}{\Longrightarrow}\; (\mathrm{G})
\;\Longrightarrow\; (\mathrm{M})
$$
:::

where $(\mathrm{M})$ is: given $f : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$, $g : \Gamma_g \to \mathbb{R}$,
$h : \Gamma_h \to \mathbb{R}$, $\underline{\underline{K}} : \Omega \to
\mathbb{R}^{n_{sd}\times n_{sd}}$, find $\underline{d}$ such that
$\underline{\underline{K}}\,\underline{d} = \underline{F}$, where

::: {.derivation}
$$
\begin{aligned}
K_{AB} &= \int_\Omega \nabla N_A \cdot \underline{\underline{K}}\nabla N_B\;d\Omega \\[6pt]
F_A &= \int_\Omega N_A f\;d\Omega + \int_{\Gamma_h} N_A h\;d\Gamma \\[2pt]
    &\qquad - \int_\Omega \nabla N_A \cdot \underline{\underline{K}}
      \left(\sum_{B \in \Gamma_g} g_B N_B\right) d\Omega
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

For a given problem, this becomes a matrix equation with $n_{unk}$ rows and $n_{unk}$
columns (note the symmetry — this will be shown to be sparse).

# A one-dimensional example

```{python fig_setup}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
```

![Three elements, lengths $\ell_0+\ell_1+\ell_2 = L$. Node $N_3$ is "known" (Dirichlet, value $g$); node $N_0$ carries the prescribed flux $h$.](`{python} fig_setup_path`){#fig-c8-setup width=80%}

## The basis functions on this mesh

The four nodes sit at $x_0 = 0$, $x_1$, $x_2$, and $x_3 = L$, and the three elements
between them have lengths $\ell_e = x_{e+1} - x_e$. Each node carries one basis function:
$N_A$ is the piecewise-linear function that is $1$ at its own node and $0$ at every other
node,

::: {.derivation}
$$
N_A(x_B) = \delta_{AB} =
\begin{cases} 1, & A = B \\ 0, & A \neq B \end{cases}
$$
:::

::: {.step}
"Linear on each element", plus that one requirement, fixes all four functions completely.
:::

```{python fig_basis}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

ELL = [l0, l1, l2]


# the i-th piecewise-linear hat: 1 at node i, 0 at every other node
def Nhat(i, xv):
    xv = np.asarray(xv, dtype=float)
    out = np.zeros_like(xv)
    if i > 0:
        m = (xv >= x[i - 1]) & (xv <= x[i])
        out[m] = (xv[m] - x[i - 1]) / (x[i] - x[i - 1])
    if i < 3:
        m = (xv >= x[i]) & (xv <= x[i + 1])
        out[m] = (x[i + 1] - xv[m]) / (x[i + 1] - x[i])
    return out


# constant value of N_{i,x} on element e: +1/l_e left of node i, -1/l_e right of it
def dval(i, e):
    if i == e + 1:
        return 1.0 / ELL[e]
    if i == e:
        return -1.0 / ELL[e]
    return 0.0


# derivative of the i-th hat, evaluated pointwise; it is undefined at the nodes
# themselves, but that jump is a set of measure zero, so no integral sees it
def dNhat(i, xv):
    xv = np.asarray(xv, dtype=float)
    out = np.zeros_like(xv)
    for e in range(3):
        m = (xv >= x[e]) & (xv < x[e + 1])
        out[m] = dval(i, e)
    return out


def hat_axes(ax):
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    ax.spines[["left", "bottom"]].set_linewidth(0.9)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=10)
    for xi in x:
        ax.axvline(xi, color=MESHCLR, lw=0.7, ls=":", alpha=0.6, zorder=1)
    ax.axhline(0, color=DIMCLR, lw=0.8, zorder=1)


xf = np.linspace(0, L, 1500)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 1, figsize=(7.4, 7.0), sharex=True)
for i, ax in enumerate(axes):
    c = BASISCLRS[i]
    yv = Nhat(i, xf)
    ax.fill_between(xf, 0, yv, color=c, alpha=0.14, lw=0, zorder=2)
    ax.plot(xf, yv, color=c, lw=2.4, zorder=4)
    hat_axes(ax)
    ax.plot(x, Nhat(i, x), "o", mfc="white", mec=c, mew=1.6, ms=6.5, zorder=5)
    ax.text(0.012, 0.92, f"$N_{i}$", transform=ax.transAxes, color=c,
            fontsize=15, va="top", ha="left")
    ax.set_ylim(-0.3, 1.38)
    ax.set_yticks([0, 1])
for e in range(3):
    axes[0].text(0.5 * (x[e] + x[e + 1]), 1.14, f"element {e}", ha="center",
                 va="bottom", fontsize=9.5, color=MESHCLR)
axes[-1].set_xticks(x)
axes[-1].set_xticklabels([f"$x_{k}$" for k in range(4)], fontsize=12)
axes[-1].set_xlabel("$x$", fontsize=12)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.5)
fig_basis_path = save(fig, "C8_Fig2_BasisFunctions.png")
```

![One basis function per plot, on the mesh of @fig-c8-setup. Each $N_A$ rises to $1$ at
its own node, falls back to $0$ at its neighbours, and is zero everywhere else. The two
end functions, $N_0$ and $N_3$, are half of a
hat.](`{python} fig_basis_path`){#fig-c8-basis width=84%}

Written out, each one is a straight line on every element it touches:

::: {.derivation}
$$
N_A(x) =
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{x - x_{A-1}}{\ell_{A-1}}, & x_{A-1} \le x \le x_A \quad (\text{if } A > 0) \\[10pt]
\dfrac{x_{A+1} - x}{\ell_A}, & x_A \le x \le x_{A+1} \quad (\text{if } A < 3) \\[10pt]
0, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
$$
:::

The end functions, $N_0$ and $N_3$, simply lose one of the two branches, because there is
no element on the far side of their node.

::: {.step}
Two properties to keep hold of: each $N_A$ is **zero outside the one or two elements that
touch node $A$** (this is what will make $\underline{\underline{K}}$ sparse), and at every
$x$ the four functions **sum to one**, $\sum_A N_A(x) = 1$.
:::

## The derivatives of the basis functions

Each branch above is linear in $x$, so each derivative is a **constant on each element**:
differentiating $(x - x_{A-1})/\ell_{A-1}$ gives $+1/\ell_{A-1}$, and differentiating
$(x_{A+1} - x)/\ell_A$ gives $-1/\ell_A$. The shorter the element, the steeper the ramp
and the larger that constant.

::: {.derivation}
$$
N_{A,x}(x) =
\begin{cases}
+\dfrac{1}{\ell_{A-1}}, & x_{A-1} < x < x_A \quad (\text{if } A > 0) \\[10pt]
-\dfrac{1}{\ell_A}, & x_A < x < x_{A+1} \quad (\text{if } A < 3) \\[10pt]
0, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
$$
:::

```{python fig_derivs}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 1, figsize=(7.4, 7.0), sharex=True)
for i, ax in enumerate(axes):
    c = BASISCLRS[i]
    hat_axes(ax)
    prev = 0.0
    for e in range(3):
        v = dval(i, e)
        if v != 0.0:
            ax.fill_between([x[e], x[e + 1]], 0, v, color=c, alpha=0.14, lw=0,
                            zorder=2)
            lab = (r"$+1/\ell_%d$" if v > 0 else r"$-1/\ell_%d$") % e
            ax.text(0.5 * (x[e] + x[e + 1]), v + (0.09 if v > 0 else -0.09), lab,
                    ha="center", va="bottom" if v > 0 else "top", color=c,
                    fontsize=12)
        ax.plot([x[e], x[e + 1]], [v, v], color=c, lw=2.4, zorder=4,
                solid_capstyle="butt")
        ax.plot([x[e], x[e]], [prev, v], color=c, lw=1.0, ls=":", zorder=3)
        prev = v
    ax.plot([x[3], x[3]], [prev, 0.0], color=c, lw=1.0, ls=":", zorder=3)
    ax.text(0.988, 0.92, f"$N_{{{i},x}}$", transform=ax.transAxes, color=c,
            fontsize=15, va="top", ha="right")
    ax.set_ylim(-1.05, 1.05)
    ax.set_yticks([0])
axes[-1].set_xticks(x)
axes[-1].set_xticklabels([f"$x_{k}$" for k in range(4)], fontsize=12)
axes[-1].set_xlabel("$x$", fontsize=12)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.5)
fig_derivs_path = save(fig, "C8_Fig3_Derivatives.png")
```

![The derivative of each basis function: one constant per element, jumping at the nodes.
The sign flips where the hat turns from rising to falling, and the size is set by the
length of the element.](`{python} fig_derivs_path`){#fig-c8-derivs width=84%}

::: {.step .notes}
- At the nodes themselves the derivative jumps and is undefined. Those are finitely many
  points, so no integral ever notices them — which is precisely why the weak form, needing
  only one derivative, is the right setting for these functions.
- On any one element the four values add to zero. That follows from $\sum_A N_A = 1$:
  differentiate both sides, and $\sum_A N_{A,x} = 0$ on every element. It is also why the
  all-node matrix below is singular until a Dirichlet value is imposed.
:::

## Writing out $\underline{\underline{K}}\,\underline{d} = \underline{F}$

::: {.derivation}
$$
\begin{bmatrix}
\int_0^L N_{0,x}N_{0,x}\,dx & \int_0^L N_{0,x}N_{1,x}\,dx & \int_0^L N_{0,x}N_{2,x}\,dx \\[4pt]
\int_0^L N_{1,x}N_{0,x}\,dx & \int_0^L N_{1,x}N_{1,x}\,dx & \int_0^L N_{1,x}N_{2,x}\,dx \\[4pt]
\int_0^L N_{2,x}N_{0,x}\,dx & \int_0^L N_{2,x}N_{1,x}\,dx & \int_0^L N_{2,x}N_{2,x}\,dx
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} d_0 \\ d_1 \\ d_2 \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix} F_0 \\ F_1 \\ F_2 \end{bmatrix}
$$
:::

::: {.derivation}
$$
\begin{aligned}
F_0 &= \int_0^L N_0 f\,dx + N_0(0)h - g\int_0^L N_{0,x}N_{3,x}\,dx \\[4pt]
F_1 &= \int_0^L N_1 f\,dx - g\int_0^L N_{1,x}N_{3,x}\,dx \\[4pt]
F_2 &= \int_0^L N_2 f\,dx - g\int_0^L N_{2,x}N_{3,x}\,dx
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

## Simplifying based on the supports of the functions

::: {.step}
$N_0$ and $N_2$ are **not adjacent** — their supports (elements 0–1 and 1–2 respectively)
share at most a single point, so $\int_\Omega N_{0,x}N_{2,x}\,d\Omega = 0$. The same holds
for $N_0$/$N_3$ and $N_1$/$N_3$. This is the origin of **sparsity**: most entries of
$K_{AB}$ vanish because most pairs of basis functions don't overlap.
:::

::: {.derivation}
$$
\begin{bmatrix}
\int_0^L N_{0,x}N_{0,x}\,dx & \int_0^L N_{0,x}N_{1,x}\,dx & 0 \\[4pt]
\int_0^L N_{1,x}N_{0,x}\,dx & \int_0^L N_{1,x}N_{1,x}\,dx & \int_0^L N_{1,x}N_{2,x}\,dx \\[4pt]
0 & \int_0^L N_{2,x}N_{1,x}\,dx & \int_0^L N_{2,x}N_{2,x}\,dx
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} d_0 \\ d_1 \\ d_2 \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix} F_0 \\ F_1 \\ F_2 \end{bmatrix}
$$
:::

::: {.derivation}
$$
\begin{aligned}
F_0 &= \int_0^L N_0 f\,dx + h \\[4pt]
F_1 &= \int_0^L N_1 f\,dx \\[4pt]
F_2 &= \int_0^L N_2 f\,dx - g\int_0^L N_{2,x}N_{3,x}\,dx
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

```{python check_sparsity}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

xq = np.linspace(0, L, 400001)[:-1]
K = np.zeros((4, 4))
for i in range(4):
    for j in range(4):
        K[i, j] = np.trapezoid(dNhat(i, xq) * dNhat(j, xq), xq)

# tridiagonal, closed-form entries for a piecewise-linear 1D stiffness matrix
# (tolerance set by the trapezoidal quadrature grid resolution, ~1/n_pts)
tol = 1e-5
assert abs(K[0, 0] - 1 / l0) < tol
assert abs(K[1, 1] - (1 / l0 + 1 / l1)) < tol
assert abs(K[2, 2] - (1 / l1 + 1 / l2)) < tol
assert abs(K[3, 3] - 1 / l2) < tol
assert abs(K[0, 1] + 1 / l0) < tol
assert abs(K[1, 2] + 1 / l1) < tol
assert abs(K[2, 3] + 1 / l2) < tol
# non-adjacent basis functions truly do not overlap
assert abs(K[0, 2]) < 1e-12 and abs(K[0, 3]) < 1e-12 and abs(K[1, 3]) < 1e-12

# the fractions quoted in the text, for l0, l1, l2 = 1.5, 2.0, 2.5
assert abs(K[0, 0] - 2 / 3) < tol and abs(K[1, 1] - 7 / 6) < tol
assert abs(K[2, 2] - 9 / 10) < tol and abs(K[3, 3] - 2 / 5) < tol
assert abs(K[0, 1] + 2 / 3) < tol and abs(K[1, 2] + 1 / 2) < tol
assert abs(K[2, 3] + 2 / 5) < tol

# partition of unity, and therefore derivatives that cancel on every element
assert np.allclose(sum(Nhat(i, xq) for i in range(4)), 1.0, atol=1e-12)
assert np.allclose(sum(dNhat(i, xq) for i in range(4)), 0.0, atol=1e-12)
assert np.allclose(K.sum(axis=1), 0.0, atol=tol)      # every row sums to zero

# assembling the three element matrices reproduces the same global matrix
Kasm = np.zeros((4, 4))
for e, le in enumerate(ELL):
    Kasm[e:e + 2, e:e + 2] += np.array([[1.0, -1.0], [-1.0, 1.0]]) / le
assert np.allclose(Kasm, K, atol=tol)
```

## Evaluating the entries

Every integrand left in $\underline{\underline{K}}$ is a product of two of the
piecewise-constant derivatives in @fig-c8-derivs. On any one element that product is
itself **a constant**, so the integral over that element is just the constant times the
element's length:

::: {.derivation}
$$
\int_{x_e}^{x_{e+1}} N_{A,x}\,N_{B,x}\;dx
= \underbrace{N_{A,x}\,N_{B,x}}_{\text{constant on element } e}\;\ell_e .
$$
:::


::: {.derivation}
$$
\begin{aligned}
K_{11} &= \int_0^L N_{1,x}N_{1,x}\,dx
= \left(\frac{1}{\ell_0}\right)^{2}\ell_0 + \left(-\frac{1}{\ell_1}\right)^{2}\ell_1
= \frac{1}{\ell_0} + \frac{1}{\ell_1}, \\[6pt]
K_{12} &= \int_0^L N_{1,x}N_{2,x}\,dx
= \left(-\frac{1}{\ell_1}\right)\left(+\frac{1}{\ell_1}\right)\ell_1
= -\frac{1}{\ell_1}, \\[6pt]
K_{02} &= \int_0^L N_{0,x}N_{2,x}\,dx = 0 .
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

::: {.step}
In general $K_{AA} = \dfrac{1}{\ell_{A-1}} + \dfrac{1}{\ell_A}$ (drop whichever term does
not exist, at the two ends), $K_{A,A+1} = K_{A+1,A} = -\dfrac{1}{\ell_A}$, and every other
entry is zero. Nothing here depends on $f$, $g$, or $h$: **the stiffness matrix is a
property of the mesh alone.**
:::

With the lengths of @fig-c8-setup, $\ell_0 = 1.5$, $\ell_1 = 2$, and $\ell_2 = 2.5$, so
$1/\ell_0 = 2/3$, $1/\ell_1 = 1/2$, and $1/\ell_2 = 2/5$. Striking out the row and column
of the Dirichlet node leaves the system that is actually solved:

::: {.derivation}
$$
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{2}{3} & -\frac{2}{3} & 0 \\[4pt]
-\frac{2}{3} & \frac{7}{6} & -\frac{1}{2} \\[4pt]
0 & -\frac{1}{2} & \frac{9}{10}
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} d_0 \\ d_1 \\ d_2 \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\int_0^L N_0 f\,dx + h \\[4pt]
\int_0^L N_1 f\,dx \\[4pt]
\int_0^L N_2 f\,dx + \frac{2}{5}\,g
\end{bmatrix}
$$
:::

::: {.step}
The $g$ term changed sign on its way across the equals sign, because the entry it came
from is negative: $-g\int_0^L N_{2,x}N_{3,x}\,dx = -g\left(-\frac{1}{\ell_2}\right)
= +\frac{g}{\ell_2}$. Every entry of the matrix is now a number. The only integrals still
standing are the ones containing $f$, and those are what quadrature is for.
:::

::: {.step}
Notice that **all the integrals in $\underline{\underline{K}}$ look the same**, in some
way:
:::

::: {.step .notes}
- Dirichlet (known) boundary-condition data looks the same as the integrals in
  $\underline{\underline{K}}$ — it is just $\int \nabla N_A \cdot
  \underline{\underline{K}} \nabla N_B$ against a *known* coefficient $g_B$.
- Neumann (known-flux) boundary-condition data is a **number** in 1D — but a **curve** in
  2D and a **surface** in 3D.
- Integrals with forcing functions on the right-hand side all look the same as each other.
:::

::: {.step}
That observation is what makes a general-purpose code possible: there are only a handful
of distinct integral shapes to implement, no matter the problem or the dimension.
:::

# The local view: appearance on a single element

```{python fig_local}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 3.4))
xi, xip1 = 0.0, 2.0
ax.plot([xi, xip1], [0, 0], color=INK, lw=2.4, zorder=2)
ax.plot([xi], [0], marker="|", color=INK, ms=12, mew=1.5, zorder=3)
ax.plot([xip1], [0], marker="|", color=INK, ms=12, mew=1.5, zorder=3)
xs = np.linspace(xi, xip1, 100)
ax.plot(xs, (xip1 - xs) / (xip1 - xi), color=BDRYCLR, lw=2.0)
ax.plot(xs, (xs - xi) / (xip1 - xi), color=LOADCLR, lw=2.0)
ax.text(xi - 0.1, 1.12, "$N_i$", color=BDRYCLR, fontsize=13, ha="center")
ax.text(xip1 + 0.1, 1.12, "$N_{i+1}$", color=LOADCLR, fontsize=13, ha="center")
# global (black) names above, local element (brown) names below -- the
# relabelling is the whole point of this figure
ax.text(xi, -0.42, "$x_i$", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=11.5, color=INK)
ax.text(xip1, -0.42, "$x_{i+1}$", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=11.5,
        color=INK)
ax.text(xi, -0.95, "$x_0^e$", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=11.5,
        color=MESHCLR)
ax.text(xip1, -0.95, "$x_1^e$", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=11.5,
        color=MESHCLR)
ax.text(xi - 0.1, 0.88, "$N_0^e$", color=MESHCLR, fontsize=12, ha="center")
ax.text(xip1 + 0.1, 0.88, "$N_1^e$", color=MESHCLR, fontsize=12, ha="center")
tidy(ax)
ax.set_xlim(-0.9, 2.9)
ax.set_ylim(-1.4, 1.4)
fig_local_path = save(fig, "C8_Fig4_LocalView.png")
```

![](`{python} fig_local_path`){#fig-c8-local width=45%}

We want to solve integrals like

::: {.derivation}
$$
\int_{x_i}^{x_{i+1}} N_{i,x}\,N_{i+1,x}\;dx = \int_{x_0^e}^{x_1^e} N_{0,x}^e\,N_{1,x}^e\;dx
$$
:::

::: {.step}
and similarly $\int_{x_i}^{x_{i+1}} N_{i+s,x}N_{i+t,x}\,dx
= \int_{x_0^e}^{x_1^e} N_{s,x}^e N_{t,x}^e\,dx$ for $s,t \in \{0,1\}$: the integral only
depends on the **local** shape of the basis functions restricted to that one element, not
on which global element it happens to be. This is why we can compute a small "element"
integral once and reuse the recipe everywhere. Likewise for load terms:
:::

::: {.derivation}
$$
\int_{x_i}^{x_{i+1}} N_i\,f\;dx = \int_{x_0^e}^{x_1^e} N_0^e\,f\;dx
\qquad
\int_{x_i}^{x_{i+1}} N_{i+1}\,f\;dx = \int_{x_0^e}^{x_1^e} N_1^e\,f\;dx
$$
:::

## The element stiffness matrix

On element $e$, of length $\ell_e = x_1^e - x_0^e$, the two local functions and their
derivatives are

::: {.derivation}
$$
\begin{aligned}
N_0^e(x) &= \frac{x_1^e - x}{\ell_e}, &\qquad N_1^e(x) &= \frac{x - x_0^e}{\ell_e}, \\[6pt]
N_{0,x}^e &= -\frac{1}{\ell_e}, &\qquad N_{1,x}^e &= +\frac{1}{\ell_e} .
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

The four local integrals $\int_{x_0^e}^{x_1^e} N_{s,x}^e N_{t,x}^e\,dx$ are then four
constants times $\ell_e$, and they fit in one small matrix:

::: {.derivation}
$$
\underline{\underline{k}}^e =
\begin{bmatrix}
\left(-\frac{1}{\ell_e}\right)^{2}\ell_e & \left(-\frac{1}{\ell_e}\right)\left(\frac{1}{\ell_e}\right)\ell_e \\[6pt]
\left(\frac{1}{\ell_e}\right)\left(-\frac{1}{\ell_e}\right)\ell_e & \left(\frac{1}{\ell_e}\right)^{2}\ell_e
\end{bmatrix}
= \frac{1}{\ell_e}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$
:::

::: {.step}
Every element of every mesh of this kind has that same matrix; only $\ell_e$ changes.
Adding each $\underline{\underline{k}}^e$ into the rows and columns of its own two nodes
rebuilds the global matrix, one element at a time — **assembly**, which
[Class 10](10_Class.qmd) takes up with the IEN array.
:::


# Numerical quadrature

Let $p(x)$ be a function. How can we solve $\int_a^b p\;dx$ in general on a computer?
$\to$ **numerical quadrature.**

::: {.step}
**Example: Riemann sums.** Sum a bunch of bins with height $h_i$, base length $B_i$:
$\sum_i h_i B_i \approx$ area/integral, where $h_i = p(x_i)$.
:::

```{python fig_riemann}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

def p(xv):
    return 1.2 + 0.5 * np.sin(1.6 * xv) + 0.15 * xv


a_, b_ = 0.2, 5.6
xf = np.linspace(a_, b_, 400)
n_bins = 9
edges = np.linspace(a_, b_, n_bins + 1)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.4))
ax.plot(xf, p(xf), color=BDRYCLR, lw=2.0, zorder=3)
for i in range(n_bins):
    xm = 0.5 * (edges[i] + edges[i + 1])
    ax.bar(edges[i], p(xm), width=edges[i + 1] - edges[i], align="edge",
           color=DOMCLR, edgecolor=MESHCLR, lw=1.0, zorder=1)
ax.text(a_, p(a_) + 0.25, "$p(x)$", color=BDRYCLR, fontsize=12)
ax.set_xlabel("$x$", fontsize=12)
ax.set_xlim(a_ - 0.1, b_ + 0.1)
ax.set_ylim(0, 2.2)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.set_xticks([a_, b_]); ax.set_xticklabels(["$a$", "$b$"])
ax.set_yticks([])
fig_riemann_path = save(fig, "C8_Fig5_Riemann.png")
```

![](`{python} fig_riemann_path`){#fig-c8-riemann width=68%}

```{python check_riemann}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

# a fine enough Riemann sum should approximate the true integral well
exact = np.trapezoid(p(np.linspace(a_, b_, 400001)), np.linspace(a_, b_, 400001))
edges_fine = np.linspace(a_, b_, 2001)
riemann = sum(p(0.5 * (edges_fine[i] + edges_fine[i + 1])) *
              (edges_fine[i + 1] - edges_fine[i]) for i in range(2000))
assert abs(riemann - exact) / abs(exact) < 1e-3
```

We want to pick some ideal choice of quadrature rule for **polynomial basis functions**:

::: {.derivation}
$$
\int_a^b p(x)\;dx = \sum_{g=0}^{n_g - 1} w_g\,p(x_g)
$$
:::

::: {.step}
for some polynomial degree, where $w_g$ and $x_g$ are special points and weights — the
subject of the next class.
:::
